lawyer:
AF Hasan Ariff with Faridul Alam Chowdhury -----For the Petitioner.
Shahabuddin Ahmad, Deputy Attorney-General -----For the Respondents.
parties:
Friends Corporation ------ Petitioner
vs
Commissioner of Customs and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
AM Mahmudur Rahman J: This Rule calls in question the levy of customs duty on the basis of tariff value instead of registration value pursuant to import particular registration scheme on the ground that imposition and levy of duty upon such basis without any lawful authority.

2. The petitioner, a firm, carries on business of import of Caustic Soda. It opened Letter of Credit on 21-1-1998 for importing 350 MT of Caustic Soda solid and 150 MT of Caustic Soda Flakes at the rate of US$ 250.00 per metric ton and 260.00 per metric ton respectively. On arrival of the consignment the petitioner through its clearing agent submitted bill of entry and certificate of registration for assessment of duties on the basis of invoice value. But respondent 2, appraiser, illegally and arbitrarily directed to assess the duties and charges on the basis of tariff value.

3. The petitioner contends that Kfixation of tariff value at US$ 375.00 per metric ton under HS Code No. 2815. 11.00 is arbitrary and baseless for the merchandise. The basis for determination of tariff value under delegated authority as provided in section 25(7) of the Customs Act, 1969 on the basis of Notification No. 38/97 Cus. dated 30-12-97 suffers from want of authority and, as such, the assessment of duty impugned is illegal. It is further contended that delegated power as conceived in section 25(7) of the Act has no relation with the normal market price and, as such, the basis for levy of duty in exercise of delegated power in the present case is without lawful authority. Farther, it was argued that sub-section (7) of section 25 is independent of other provisions of the section and there being no guideline for determination for fixing tariff value the impugned order is arbitrary and without lawful authority. It is further contended that as the petitioner being allured by the notification pursuant to import registration scheme dated 12-6- 97 opened letter of credit for import of the merchandise the customs authority imposed duty on tariff value against doctrine of promissory estoppel.

4. The learned Deputy Attorney-General, on the other hand, drawing our attention to the scheme itself argued that scheme provides that the exporter at least during 3 years is to export commodities to the tune of Taka 5 crore in order to obtain registration under the scheme. He drew our attention to the figure containing the export value for the year 1995-96 and 96-97 and submitted that it did not reach the target of Taka 5 crore. He also argued that mere registration is not enough to get the special benefit under the scheme. He contends that unless the price given by the exporter is approved by the registration authority, the customs authority has got sufficient power to determine the value of the merchandise on the basis of tariff value.

5. Before we enter into the contention we are inclined to examine the law itself. The Customs Act, 1969 has elaborately dealt with fixation of the price of imported goods, determination of tariff value, levy of customs duty. Section 25 is on value of the imported and exported goods. Sub-section (2) of this section provides for determination of normal price of any imported goods and for such determination certain conditions are to be followed section 30 is on the dated for determination of the value and rate of import duty. Section 30A which was inserted on July 1, 1995 is on value and effective rate of duty. According to sub-section (1) of section 25 normal value means price which the commodity would fetch on the date referred to in section 30 on a sale in open market between a buyer and seller independent of each other. The contention that as the petitioner on the basis of import registration scheme opened Letter of Credit and the invoice, supplied by the exporter mentioning price at a lower rate the duty assessed by the Customs authority on the basis of tariff value is without any sanction of law. This leads us to consider the provision of section 30A. Section 30A reads:

"30A Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or any decision of any court for the purposes of section 30, the value and the rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively include the value as determined under section 25 and any amount of duty imposed under section 18, 18A or 18B and the amount of duties that may have become payable in consequence of the withdrawal of the whole or any part of the exemption or concession from duty whether before or after the conclusion of a contract or agreement for the sale 0 such goods or opening of a letter of credit in respect thereof".

<u>6. Section 30A sufficiently indicates that notwithstanding anything contained in the Customs Act the value and rate of duty applicable to any goods shall include the value as determined under section 25 of the Act whether or after opening the LC in respect of the goods. Although LC was opened pursuant to scheme which came into force on 12-6-97 but opening Letter of Credit is subject to section 30A for the expressions. "Whether or after" opening the Letter of Credit in respect thereof in section 30A of the Customs Act, 1969 which does not admit of any ambiguity. The expression "thereof’’ is of wide connotation and it includes any goods and the rate of duty is applicable to any goods. Therefore, cumulative effect of reading of sections 25(7), 30 and 30A together is that the levy of duty on the basis of tariff value giving go-by to the scheme and the rate as shown in the invoice by the exporter has been levied legally, properly and with lawful authority. Mr. Hasan Ariff contends also that other provision of law provides that if the ex-parte and importer give the higher value than the tariff value then higher value will be determined for assessing the duty and where the invoice value is less than the tariff value the determining factor for assessing customs duty is the invoice value. We cannot read such thing in section 25(7). We do not find any want of jurisdiction under section 25(7) on the part of the customs authority to assess the duty under challenge.</u>

7. A careful consideration of section 25A indicates that it contains provision for guideline to be made by notification in the form of SRO Therefore, in this case for the aforesaid provision of law vis-a-vis the Registration Import Particular Scheme we do not find any want of authority on the part of the respondent to assess the duty on the basis of tariff value. Secondly, we are called upon to decide whether the petitioner is entitled to the benefit under import Particular Registration Scheme dated 12-6-97. The Scheme says that any exporter is entitled to the benefit on fulfillment of the condition laid down therein. The petitioner filed an application for such relief under the Scheme. But the conditions could not be fulfilled. Therefore, the contention on the doctrine of promissory estoppel has got no role to play in the facts of this case. The principle laid down in Mannan's case, 42DLR 107 (AD), has no role to play in the present case inasmuch as section 30A was not on the statute when the Appellate Division decided the Mannan's case and that too was made on dissimilar-facts. By subsequent insertion of section 30A of the Customs Act, 1969 the mischief, want of authority, by the Parliament in subsection (7) of section 25 of the Act which was in existence has been removed, Thus, the contention that in the absence of any guideline no action can be taken as has been taken by the impugned order of assessment of levy of duty has no leg to stand. The observation made by the High Court Division in Nasiruddin case is merely an obiter and does not lay down any principle of law having any binding legal force. Moreover, in view of insertion of section 30A as has been held in the case of Collector of Customs vs Ahmed Hossain & others, 48 DLR 199 (AD), the contention seems to be bereft of any substance.

8. Mr. Deputy Attorney-General opposes this Rule on the ground of maintainability. He submits that as the petitioner himself stated that he having had taken appeal without exhausting that remedy this petition is not maintainable. We are also of the view that as the petitioner filed appeal against the order under challenge in this Rule without disposal of the appeal the Writ Petition is not maintainable and we should not exercise our jurisdiction as conferred under Article 102 of the Constitution in the instant case.

For the aforesaid reason, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.
